video_title: Aydin Senkut: Chasing Demand, Not Hype, at Felicis
transcript: [music] [music] >> Aydin, thanks so much for joining me. >> Ted, thanks for having me. >> So, it's been a few years since you came on, and more importantly, 20 years since you started Felicis. And I thought it'd be fun to start with just this open-ended question of as you look at the landscape and how you're investing today, what's changed and evolved over these 20 years since you started? >> One of the things that I think especially most important for Felicis we are a firm with a growth mindset and our most important top cultural value is learning and adapting rapidly. So, we have kind of built change into the DNA of the firm. And one of the reasons we did that, we're generalist investors, and I wanted to do that because at the end, there are a lot of exciting companies that come up in technology, and a lot of it happens because of disruption, and the disruption happens really fast. And I always wanted us to have the option of being able to choose the markets where we feel the biggest growth is happening, where we feel the biggest future potential is. So, we have always used that generalist strategy, and we put it to great use and, you know, started in consumer internet right when I left Google, then shifted to e-commerce and fintech with Shopify and Credit Karma and Plaid, and then later on to SaaS, some great SaaS companies, and most recently a lot of AI infrastructure companies, web security, uh, global resilience and beyond. That's what changed. What has not changed is we've always been early stage focused. Even today, with a larger fund close to a billion dollars, 91% of our investments are seed and Series A. And then the last aspect of it, every venture firm I think needs a core differentiation, and one of the reasons why founders choose us is because we have conviction and we've been able to show that conviction more rapidly than other firms. And then we have always demonstrated that we earn the trust. So we have two initiatives that really helped us. So one of the things that did not change in those 20 years is to always be, you know, try to be an attempt to be the founder's most trusted partner in venture capital and earn their trust and their partnership through our ability to show conviction better and faster than others. >> What has that looked like over the years? So as a concept, it's great. You're going to go ahead of where the puck's moving. You're going to be there before everybody. You're going to be helpful. You're covering the world. You're trying to find the biggest growth areas. How have you evolved to doing that better and better as the years have gone on? >> We're surfing these waves and these these waves we we we like to find if each one of these waves is like a technological trend, you know, we're trying to find the best companies, find the best waves, surf it to great returns. I think this is now turned into there are so many waves and surfers we are trying to go for the tsunami waves. At the end of the day, our business is very simple. We need to generate growth that is so far beyond you can get in public markets and do that before it's obvious to most other people. The way we like to do that is we like to find companies where we can plausibly call out at least 100x revenue growth from the point we invest in or more. And it's all about playing the probabilities. Obviously, some of these things if it was like super easy to get, most everyone would be in those companies. But what we're looking for is like is there enough market size? Is there enough demand? We like to chase demand. So is there enough demand to justify at least 100x revenue growth or beyond? And we have done that consistently. And what we like to do is things in in the world are changing really fast. Like I would say, you know, two years ago, three years ago, not a lot of people were talking about defense or even certain aspects of AI or global resilience. And I would say in the last three years we have realized, know, we need a lot better and scalable solutions for energy. Defense is not going to go away. The conflicts are here to stay. We need to do a better job at that. And in terms of AI, like one of the things that is an area where a lot of people have pivoted in, but we have also found that there are like derivative areas that are still benefiting that are not necessarily just model companies. Like the most important raw material for AI is data. We have a bunch of data companies. You know, they tend to use a lot of data center resources and all of that. So all we try to do is if you chase the right demand, we feel the revenue growth will follow. And if the revenue growth follows, then the valuation will follow. I think what happens is a lot of times people are trying to look at the signal and the demand and like the hot companies, but instead of chasing the demand, they can sometimes chase hype. So we try to really pay attention to where the demand is coming from and we base our decisions on the real business performance of the companies and reality catches on. Like a good example is we invested in Super Base right at the top of the 2021 kind of like valuation peak. And it took us two to three years to for the market to catch on, but the company's business performance has grown like almost 3,000 X since we invested. So it took three years for the market valuation to reflect what's actually been happening. And then all of a sudden it started taking off really fast. So if you only look at valuation, you feel like, oh, that company has been stagnant for three years and then all of a sudden something happened. But if you look at the underlying business growth has been very steady and accelerating year after year. And so that's why we like to look at the underlying business performance because if that business performance is really strong and growth is accelerating, sooner or later the market valuation will catch up to that as well. >> What you're describing is this difference between the fundamentals and at times a price, or you said hype, that may already reflect a few years of those fundamentals coming through. Talk to me about an example of something where those two things were disconnected, where the hype was just way ahead of the underlying growth of something that you chose not to invest in. >> I mean, there has been many areas uh where we chose not to invest. For instance, like being an ex-Google investor, I was very skeptical about marketing and ad tech companies. I felt like even if there are some interesting growth spurts at the end, once I left Google and I saw Google and Facebook, especially like in consumer companies, it's so difficult. The bar is now a billion users and there are companies already with great ad networks. It's very difficult to build that. I mean, recently we are now in a new world where because of AI, anybody can build any piece of software and customize it and the bar to developing custom software has gone down so much. Now like you have to really look and say, where do you invest in a world where creating software is no longer really that difficult? Now there is fundamental pieces of software that still matters and all of that, but all in all like that's one of the reasons you're seeing some big changes in the SaaS world. And then I would say like one of the things uh that changed in my mind in a different way um is the interesting trends that also supporting more capital intensive technology areas than capital light technology areas. So when I started investing, I thought all, you know, software is capital light. This is really great, but now we're starting to solve much more interesting world problems and we're starting to see very interesting companies that are not capital light, but I think have still as strong, if not stronger, upside potential. >> So walk me through something that is both capital intensive and you can see the potential for a 1,000x growth, which usually just the capital intensity makes scaling much harder than in just a virtual platform. >> I have a great example for you. One of the areas we're really bullish on is robotics and physical AI. One of the reasons we're bullish on robotics, by the way, one of the interesting example is, hey, if you're curious about cool ways to catch, watch a lot of sci-fi movies and read sci-fi books, and virtually almost all of them have robots in them. I thought about it differently and I said, look, let's look at the low wage labor market. Just US, Western Europe, Japan alone, we're talking about 190 million low skilled jobs. And like that I I'm assuming like 20 to 25k per year. And you know, these robots can do this job. And so I thought, hey, like what if if the robotics company we invested that is already gaining incredible projects with Fortune 100 companies or top companies in S&P 500, they just got like 0.1 0.2% of this market, which is a tiny tiny part of this, right? 0.2% of that market would equal to 10 billion in revenues. So on the one hand, the these companies are going to require a lot of capital cuz robotics is not capital like. You need to not only just build the models, but you also need to scale that across all kinds of robots and deployment. But on the other hand, I feel like the demand is so vast. By the way, I only took the market for current low skilled labor. If all of a sudden we had robots that could do jobs 24/7 reliably, all of a sudden it might open up whole new areas where you normally would not have humans do things, you might have robots do things. So this is without even considering how much the market can expand, right? Like I remember the days where we used to use Nokia phones with nine buttons, 12 buttons, and everybody's like, oh, this is as big as like the cell you know, cell phone market is going to go. And then Apple comes up with iPhone and Android comes out and all of a sudden, I mean, you're seeing Apple is a $5 trillion company, Google is a like, you know, around $5 trillion company. So I feel like going back, this is an interesting area where on the one hand, a lot of robotics companies have failed in the past, but this new wave of robotics I feel is going to be as big of a chat GPT moment if not bigger moving into the future. And we're very bullish on it. >> When you have that belief of the growth of that sector, how do you then go from there to identifying which companies, which economic models, which founders you want to back within it? >> We have several different ways we go about it. One is, you know, finding the most obvious companies that are going to be the leaders. And in that, we're looking for original IP and durable IP. One of the things that matters is you don't want to just see high revenue growth, but you want to see durable revenue growth. And I feel one of the key ingredients to durable revenue growth is core IP that is not difficult to replicate and copy. For instance, we made our bet in a robotics company called skill.ai. Skill.ai is a very interesting company that was built by two professors that were each Facebook VP and they were Carnegie Mellon professors. We found them they're I think the most quoted people ever in robotics. Their papers have been quoted like they're the number one. If you do a research in this archive of all the all the papers, they had an idea that one of the interesting ways to solve this was with synthetic data. They were one of the first to incorporate reinforcement learning and they hired some amazing people including from Tesla. So if you combine like these are very difficult things to do, getting the best talent in the world, having not one but maybe like even two ideas that nobody else is seeing yet, applying that in a way where it makes difference, I feel like this is a really great company. So consider it is like this is kind of the equivalent of our OpenAI or Entropic bet in robotics. But that's not where it stops. There is also like huge demand for data. If robotics take off, there's going to be huge demand for robotics parts. They use actuators. You know, there's been a lot of parts and a lot of these parts are not made in the US. So we just recently signed a term sheet to invest in a company that's going to be making, you know, parts for these robotics and they can scale it. And we're also looking for a bunch of companies that could be data in robotics. So we have done really well in the AI wave back in companies like Mercor that basically supply the data to essentially improve these models and that business has grown incredibly by leaps and bounds. Probably the fastest growing company ever in our portfolio. We also feel there will be similar companies in robotics and beyond. >> When you have a theme like that, you're looking for the anchor company in the space, the ancillary companies that are benefiting from it. How do you balance that with backing the right founders? >> If it was really easy, everybody would be doing a perfect job and clearly it's not because there is also the tension of you want to invest early enough, especially in this new age of valuations jumping 10x instead of 2x between the rounds of great companies. So there is incredible pressure to be early in these companies and yet if you're too early and somebody else comes to the market with a better, more durable idea or better IP, obviously they're also going to be able to come into the market and capture a lot more value. I mean at the end, it's basically a probability game. You cannot just wait until things are obvious and one of the ways we balance it is, look, nobody has the crystal ball. Nobody can say that they have the answer for sure. What we try to do is look at as many fundamentals as possible. We call it multitude of signal. Just like you have a lot of really great concepts, like I remember like a narrative workshop we did and there was like, hey, these are like four or the five tenets of a great narrative. We feel like let's say there are four five elements what makes a great company and you can just say, hey, like each company has maybe one or two signals, but if a company has three signals or four signals, you know, let's go all in and we try to like capital adjust to that risk or the level of, you know, signal that we have, the multitude of signal. The other thing is to try to play the wave in as many different ways as possible. Most people think, oh, like if we're going to make a bet, we're only going to make a bet in a model company. They don't think of other elements like in robotics. Well, there's going to be a data element. There's going to be a manufacturing element. Maybe there's going to be some other elements. There might be a sovereign element, right? We are now in a different world where I would say five to 10 years ago, the sovereignty didn't matter and they were always global companies. Now for key areas like energy, AI, maybe robotics, maybe each like area, each continent will want to have their own champion. They're not going to be just satisfied with a champion, you know, from the US or Europe or whatever. And for different national security reasons as others, they might want to have a national champion as well. It's not mutually exclusive. So like I said, there might be three, four, five ways to play the same wave and we feel like the more you do that, you bring resiliency to that wave versus just making one bet because if something happens and some other company comes in, but if you basically like have also invested in the foundational companies, then whoever ends up winning, you end up winning. A great example of that is a bet we made in Superbase. So for instance, there are some very successful companies that have grown revenues like Lovable and Replit kind of chasing the citizen developers. I feel like it's a very hard area because these companies are doing a really good job and fiercely competing with each other. And I feel even though we have not backed them, a lot of these companies, virtually all of them like use Superbase is the underlying database. So in some ways, we didn't really have to make one of those bets. We still won because the company we backed that is the underlying infrastructure layer, which is Superbase, is benefiting from the sprints of these companies and the growth spurts. So I think that's how we think about it. And if if if I was to like boil down all of Felicis's 20 years of what worked out the best for us, we have always chased high demand ahead of revenue growth materializing and virtually all of our major fund maker companies have been foundational layer infra companies. Like Shopify was commerce infrastructure, Adyen was payment infrastructure, Credit Karma was credit score infrastructure. Uh we've made a lot of investments like SendGrid and other and web security that was like application, like code, security infrastructure, and AI like foundational model companies that have become like Runway and you know others that that have become underlying layer for a certain area of AI. So every time we have chosen a great infrastructure or foundational layer company, um those tend to be the ones that had the biggest upside. >> What's different in underwriting as you're moving towards say capital intensive businesses, whether it's the data side, energy, things like that, from your SaaS of the old days or AI with this infinite scaling potential? >> It is different in a few aspects. First of all, we are in a new world. I like to call it trillion dollar markets with billion dollar uh contracts. Um and what is happening is you have these areas like whether it's robotics or AI infrastructure, the demand is well documented to be around trillion dollars. And now like you have companies because of like the giants that are getting created, whether it's a chip company or a defense company, there is proven trillion dollar demand. And a few companies are getting contracts or LOI or interest over the years that are like 100 million, couple hundred million, a billion dollars. So what is end up happening is you get to a billion dollars of revenue scale a lot faster, but it's a lot more concentrated. And it might be preceded by a few years of capital investments until you get the platform ready. So on the one hand, there's a lot of interest whether it's chips, defense, and other stuff, but on the other hand, you have a much more complex product. And so this is not something that in the software like people could hack it in a weekend or like a couple months. It was asset light, you know you just had bunch of programmers, but now it's different. Like we're talking about serious hardware, very complex, uh not easy. But on the other hand, if you get it right, there is a huge payoff. There is customer concentration, but the scale and the speed with which companies scale, the magnitude of things like the speed could be an order of magnitude bigger, the scale could be an order of magnitude bigger. Obviously, there's also more capital, so you need to kind of take that into consideration and underwriting that, hey, this might need to be more than one round investment. We might need to maybe but, you know, think about reserves a little bit differently than we originally did with software companies. >> In the environment we're in today, where there's just a lot more capital looking for these types of high power law opportunities, how have you thought about how you're competing and participating when there's so much more capital looking for these ideas? >> I think overall, a quick comment on that. On the one hand, I'm glad the industry has scaled and grown, uh but on the other hand, the abundance of capital has kind of become a tax almost because at the end, when you have that much capital chasing fewer companies, it's inevitable that ownership is going to decline, valuation's going to increase. So it becomes more and more important and imperative that you find the right companies and you find them as early as possible um to make sure that we can continue those returns. So um I think there are some things that change and some things that don't. For instance, for the 20 years we've been in existence, at least for the last 10 12 years, we do a founder survey and we ask the founders, hey, what are the dimensions or what are the elements that are most important to you that influences your decision to choose a venture capital partner? And the number one and two, sometimes they they change like two and one and one and two, but over the years, it's always been pretty consistent. They really want to trust like trust is an important element. If let let's say that there is five firms or 10 firms, the firm that they trust the most, that will be one of the top three reasons. The second one is level of conviction and speed of conviction. So on the one hand, you can say we're on a new era where there is so much capital and, you know, things are changing and things are capital heavy instead of capital light, but the way the founders make decisions has not changed that much. They're still looking for have you done the homework? How strong is your conviction? How can you back out the conviction? It's almost like a job interview. It's not necessary. It used to be that founders came to investors, this is the reason you should invest in my company. Now venture capitalists are going to the founders like this is the reason you should take our money. We've done our homework. This is why we have conviction. This is what we think could the future could look like and this is why we want to partner with you. I think we have done a really good job and then the last thing is the founders want to make sure the venture partner, the venture capital firm they're partnering with is going to be able to support them. And I think that's another area where we have to keep earning their trust and I think we've done a really good job because we can tell the founders that love us become references for the new ones that we need to win. And as long as that continues, I think that's one of the other really important elements of a venture capital firm and the reputation of if you do right by the founders, the work gets around and it affects the kind of companies you can invest in, the kind of companies you can win. >> In the last few years, what are some of the examples of ways you've worked with your portfolio companies to continue to build that trust? >> I mean, honestly, the number one thing that we hold dear is that we treat every founder as individual. I think there is a temptation because of scale and because of all this like amazing dollars that are aggregating. Hey, we have a platform team and they're just going to do everything for you. And in reality, what happens is these people were not involved in writing the checks. So they try to like fix things, you know, after the check is written. We have done a couple things that are different. First of all, we always start with a question of if we can help you, what is the most important thing that we can do that you care about? I think asking that question is really important because at the end, every founder can ask us like five things, 10 things, 20 things. To me, what matters is if I could do only one of those, what is the most important thing so that if I do really, really well, then I know it's going to matter. And the other thing that I'm trying to do with that or we're trying to do as a firm is like set the expectation right so that you are much more likely to exceed the expectation versus promising, oh, we're going to do a great job with 20 and then you do 10 and the founder is like, you've done only half of what you promised me. And in reality, nobody can do like 20 items for each company they back. At the end, you're going to have to like choose the few things that matter and do a really good job. The second thing that also matters is to have trust with the founders. So sometimes the contribution is not like, oh, you helped me hire, you need you you know, you helped me do this, but also like in tough times like giving advice that is maybe contrary to what people are reading on X and you know, social media. And in order for that to work, the founders need to trust you. And by the way, that is not going to happen because you're on their board. In In fact, sometimes it's the opposite. They're actually afraid to tell you all the things because you're on the board. So one of the other things that we try to do that we go to extreme lengths with the founder pledge, with our voting pledge, what we tell the founders is, look, we're never going to vote against you. So you might as well tell us everything about the company or everything that's going on. Let's talk about the hard things. And I feel that sometimes when we can really be effective. And then finally, one thing that we like to do, we also like to be unconventional. And one of the things that we do or I would say two of the things, first, our platform team gets involved before we write a check. Imagine if you were the leader of the platform team at Felicis and we said, hey Ted, you're not going to touch any of the things we invest, but after we invest, you can come in and do your job. That is not very rewarding at the end. Investment firms, they're always investment driven. So one of the things we said is, look, why are you waiting until we write a check? Become part of the check writing process. You're a true believer then. You know exactly why we're doing it. So the other thing that happens is, then when our team follows through, um, the people that are helping are true believers in the company. You're not doing it because it's your job, because somebody else wrote the check. You're trying to save them. You're doing it because you were there in the very beginning. You were part of the decision-making process. So, I feel everybody from the investment team to everybody else in the firm that helped the founders have high agency and high belief, and then everything they do tends to be so much more effective because of that. >> So, if we circle back to the first one, identifying what's the most important thing for the founders and working on that, of those categories of things you've heard are the most important, how has that been changing over the last few years? >> I mean, there are certain things that every founder tells you like, hey, like we need to hire this person or I need to get a customer intro, whatever. One of the things that I found, one of my obsession is with strategy and instrumentation. And so, sometimes what I do with the founders is, look, I mean, I think like some of your favorite workshops or the sessions, instead of like immediately going and tackling a problem, why don't we figure out what is the most important problem to solve? Sometimes it's like they're not even realizing, but the instrumentation is not there. They have this big vision, they have this big dream, and then my question is, well, how do you know we're achieving that dream? How would you measure that? Or, um, hey, how do we know that the priorities are right? Is it really that important that we going to go after this role X? Or should we look at it and say, is that really the most important role that the company can go after? Or is there something even more important? Maybe there is a distribution deal that's important. So, one of the things that I like to do is, it's a little bit like playing chess. You're like, hey, like it's like round three, round five. Am I going to move the bishop to here? And I'm like, no, let's think about the end game. What are we really trying to do here? How are we going to get to checkmate? You know, like it might be that, hey, we might have to sacrifice couple of pawns and let's not do the obvious move, but there might be something else. So, one of the things that I try to do, whether I'm on the board or close advisor to the founders, is also to listen to them carefully, but if I feel like there is something bigger or bigger picture or higher level, that's what I like to bring to them. And my benefit is to see not just their company, but a bunch of really incredible companies. And there has been many instances where a founder has been like, we're doing really great. And I'm like, actually, I can pretty much tell you in isolated case of your company, yes, but in a group of companies in our fund where you are, you know, let's say that you're actually like 58th percentile. And so this is also really helpful to the founders because if I on an isolated basis, they might think, wow, like this is 3x growth, but hey, like you're in a vintage where 3x growth is like 58th percentile in a book of great companies across different sectors and different geos. Um so these are the kind of things that are subtle, not as obvious, but very important to lay a great foundation for these companies to continue, you know, their journey towards being the best in their areas and their sectors. >> What are some of the most recent issues that have come across your plate as things that are most important to work on today? >> I think one of the most important thing is a lot of times I love our founders. There is always like a tendency to look at what you're reading on X and social media and all like the market is moving really fast and so and so is right, you know, raising this much money. I think a lot of times what I basically tell them is look, there is not a certain formula where you get to X number at X percentage growth last year and all of a sudden the next round is going to materialize. What I try to work with them is I always call this, hey, don't show me the numbers, show me the growth formula. Have we engineered the growth formula and how durable is that growth formula? And a lot of times what I'll tell them like, look, I know you're not going to like to hear what I'm going to say, but I'm like, wait a little bit more. Maybe we need like a big distribution deal or we need like to launch a self-serve product or something like that where you know it's going to be a step function in the revenues more than the numbers and the growth figures themselves. Let's make sure that we have engineered the fundamentals because if we engineer the fundamentals, the rest is going to follow. So a lot of times we are also kind of like part coach, you know, part advisor, part helper, part psychologist. And what we're basically trying to do is look, just because something is happening in the market doesn't mean you need to blindly follow it. Like you also need to look at the fundamentals and say if we don't have the fundamentals, we might need more time. A lot of it is like just don't rush. Like do we really have to make this decision now? Like if we rush into it and we are not ready, it might be worse than waiting longer and doing it the right way because the other thing I tell them is like sometimes when you go into the market and it's premature, you're not going to get a second or third shot and say, oh, oops, that was not right. Let's do it again 6 to 12 months. People might not want to listen to you, you know, if if that's the case. So a lot of it is again reflecting and years and years. Now I can say at least two decades of experience as an investor and another decade as an operator is to essentially help them with blind spots, help them with stuff that is not necessarily obvious and make sure that they don't fall into those traps or those, you know, they don't hit on those mines. >> As you're trying to give them that advice based on your experience, let's say it's the example of saying, well, let's slow down on a capital raise and get that growth model going the right way. When you're facing a market that has an abundance of capital and there's some thought, well, maybe we should just get the capital that we're going to need in the future while it's there. How do you help a manager of a company or how do you help a founder balance that tradeoff between getting the capital while it's there and they're excited to do it and then trying to get them to listen to you >> Yeah. >> to slow down, which isn't where the market's been going. >> It's a balance question and part of the timing is, look, I think these things are sometimes a little bit of science, but also a little bit of art. And a little bit of art is you can kind of tell by the demand and heat in the market whether this idea of, hey, the market is really moving, we need to do this. I think the more important thing is not just what the founders feel, but to see how much market validation there is. So even if you do an incredible job in positioning and narrative and get everything right, and this is where like the wave surfing analogy really comes in. You know, like sometimes when you're just a little bit early, you miss the wave. You're a little bit too fast. You don't you're not in the sweet spot in the wave. So some of it is like, look, you can think about all the fundamentals, but there is also this art of like just like being there just when like the supply and demand of capital is at the right point. So and this is where like we have real-time data and we know all the investors and one of the things we try to do is the same way that we try to chase demand when making investments. I mean, we know all these funds and all the partners and we try to get ahead of things before a fund raise happens. Our job is to know where the heat is, right? Like what are the partners actually paying attention to? What are they investing in? So that we are not missing something that's obvious and we can lead tell the founders like, oh, you might like firm X, Y and Z, but in reality, they don't really care about the sector as much or this is not something they're going to get really excited. And so we can give them some market intelligence, um some other data that maybe at least like help cover some of the obvious things that is not always easy, you know, to kind of do from a founder's perspective as they're really focused on operating. >> Since you're work alongside a founder, you're going down this path, and let's just say as an example, which I'm sure you've come across, times where you just have a different opinion about what you think is the right thing for the founder and they keep acting in a way that doesn't agree with you, but you've also held this stick back which says we're always going to vote with you as a founder. So how do you behave then as a part owner of this business when the founder just seems to not be listening to what you think is the right thing to do? >> What I have learned over the years is even let's say that I know I'm right and we have a stick, I do not like using this stick because even if you're like rightfully trying to use the stick, at the end of the day, even if you're right, it leaves like a really bad feeling with the founder and instead of actually being functional, it ends up sometimes creating more chaos. I think what we try to do is at least tell them number one, what we try to do is if we're going to tell them something, we go to extreme lengths. It's not like he said, she said. It's not like I didn't said and this is it. We try to show them data. One of the things that I found is that the founders, all the founders we work with are very smart. If you go to them with an opinion, they might react and debate. If you go to them with data, chances are they're going to listen more carefully because data is harder to refute.
